statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a [proper morphism](c:is-proper) of schemes, $g\colon Y' \to Y$ a morphism, and $f'\colon X' \to Y'$, $g'\colon X' \to X$ the base change. For every torsion abelian [sheaf](c:sheaf) $\mathcal F$ on the étale site of $X$, the [base change](c:base-change) map $g^{-1}Rf_*\mathcal F \to Rf'_*g'^{-1}\mathcal F$ is an isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: The morphism $f\colon X \to Y$ is a [proper morphism](c:is-proper) of schemes.
The étale [sheaf](c:sheaf) $\mathcal F$ on $X$ is an abelian torsion sheaf.

conclusion: The base change map is an isomorphism in the derived category, so [étale cohomology](c:etale-cohomology) of torsion sheaves commutes with base change along proper maps.

proofs.name: Reduction to the projective line
proofs.slogan: Check the map on stalks, reduce proper morphisms to the projective line, and compare cohomology over a strictly henselian base with that of the closed fibre.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof (SGA 4 XII; Stacks Project, Tag 095S); the comparison over a henselian base rests on the cited text. The sheaf $\mathcal F$ has no finiteness or constructibility assumption.

roles.why: A [proper morphism](c:is-proper) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, which gives the stalk formula, and it allows the reduction to $\mathbf P^1$.
Torsion of the [sheaf](c:sheaf) is what makes the closed fibre carry the cohomology over a henselian base.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to stalks at geometric points of $Y'$.
steps.detail: A map in the derived category of étale sheaves is an isomorphism when it is one on every geometric stalk. Because $f$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, the stalks of both sides are cohomology groups over strict henselizations of $Y$ and $Y'$. So it suffices to compare these groups.

steps.slogan: Settle the case of finite morphisms first.
steps.detail: For finite $f$ the direct image is exact, and its stalk at a geometric point is the product of the stalks over the finitely many points of the fibre. So the base change map is an isomorphism, with no higher direct images. The cited text records this case as a building block.

steps.slogan: Reduce proper morphisms to the projective line over an arbitrary base.
steps.detail: The cited text shows that, if the theorem holds for $\mathbf P^1_S \to S$ for every scheme $S$, then it holds for every proper morphism. It reduces to curves by rational maps and blow-ups, and it handles the finite parts by the previous step.

steps.slogan: Compare cohomology on $\mathbf P^1$ over a strictly henselian base with that of the closed fibre.
steps.detail: For a henselian pair and a proper scheme over it, global sections of a sheaf equal those on the closed fibre. The cited text extends this comparison to all cohomology degrees of torsion sheaves on $\mathbf P^1_S$, where $S$ is strictly henselian local.

steps.slogan: Assemble the stalk comparisons into an isomorphism for every proper morphism.
steps.detail: The henselian comparison gives the stalk statement for $\mathbf P^1_S$, the reduction passes it to every proper $f$, and the first step turns the stalk statement into an isomorphism of the base change map.

concepts.c:is-proper: Properness gives the stalk formula and the reduction to the projective line.
concepts.c:sheaf: The theorem concerns torsion étale sheaves and their derived direct images.
concepts.c:base-change: The base change map is the comparison that the theorem proves to be an isomorphism.
concepts.c:etale-cohomology: Cohomology of the étale site is what the stalks compute.

source.ref: M. Artin, A. Grothendieck and J.-L. Verdier (eds.), Théorie des topos et cohomologie étale des schémas (SGA 4), tome 3, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 305, Springer, 1973, exposé XII, théorème 5.1; a modern account is The Stacks Project, section 59.91 (Tag 095S)
source.note: The Stacks Project proves the theorem by the reduction to the projective line and the henselian comparison, following SGA 4 XII with simplifications of Gabber.

statement: Let $X$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold). Sending a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) $E$ with a [flat connection](c:flat-connection) $\nabla$ to its sheaf $E^\nabla$ of horizontal sections is an [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) onto the [local systems](c:local-system) of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces on $X$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold).
The sheaf $E$ is a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) of finite rank $r$ on $X$.
The holomorphic connection $\nabla$ on $E$ is [flat](c:flat-connection): its curvature is zero.

conclusion: The horizontal sections $E^\nabla$ form a [local system](c:local-system) of rank $r$, and the functor has quasi-inverse $L \mapsto (L \otimes_{\mathbb C} \mathcal O_X,\ \mathrm{id} \otimes d)$.

proofs.name: Parallel frames and the tensor construction
proofs.slogan: Flatness gives local frames of parallel sections, so horizontal sections form a local system, and tensoring a local system with the structure sheaf gives the inverse.
proofs.scope: The basic form for holomorphic flat bundles on any complex manifold. The correspondence of regular holonomic D-modules with perverse sheaves is a separate, deeper theorem.

roles.why: Holomorphic coordinates on the [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) allow the local integration of the system, and $\mathcal O_X$ supplies the inverse construction.
A local holomorphic frame of the [bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) turns the connection into a matrix of forms.
Zero curvature is the integrability condition that yields the parallel frame.

steps.slogan: Find a frame of parallel sections near each point.
steps.detail: In a local holomorphic frame write $\nabla = d + A$ with $A$ a matrix of holomorphic 1-forms. [Flatness](c:flat-connection) gives $dA + A \wedge A = 0$, the integrability condition of the system $d\Phi = -A\Phi$. The holomorphic Frobenius theorem gives an invertible solution $\Phi$ on a small polydisc, and its columns are horizontal sections that form a frame.

steps.slogan: Show that the horizontal sections form a locally constant sheaf of rank $r$.
steps.detail:
In the parallel frame $e_1, \dots, e_r$ a section $s = \sum f_i e_i$ has $
abla s = \sum df_i\, e_i$. So $
abla s = 0$ exactly when every $f_i$ is locally constant. Hence $E^
abla \cong \mathbb C^r$ locally, and $E^
abla \otimes \mathcal O_X 	o E$ is an isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Show that the functor $E \mapsto E^\nabla$ is fully faithful.
steps.detail: A horizontal bundle map sends horizontal sections to horizontal sections, so it gives a map of local systems. Conversely a map $\lambda\colon L \to L'$ gives $\lambda \otimes \mathrm{id}$, which commutes with $d$. Since $E^\nabla \otimes \mathcal O_X \cong E$, a horizontal map is determined by its action on $E^\nabla$, so the two assignments are inverse.

steps.slogan: Build a flat bundle from each local system.
steps.detail: For a [local system](c:local-system) $L$ put $E = L \otimes_{\mathbb C} \mathcal O_X$ and $\nabla = \mathrm{id} \otimes d$. This is a holomorphic bundle with $\nabla^2 = 0$, because $d^2 = 0$. Its horizontal sections are $L \otimes \ker d = L$, since $\ker(d\colon \mathcal O_X \to \Omega^1_X)$ is the sheaf of locally constant functions.

steps.slogan: Combine full faithfulness and the inverse construction into an equivalence.
steps.detail: By the second step the functor lands in local systems of rank $r$. It is fully faithful, and every local system is isomorphic to $E^\nabla$ for the bundle just built, so it is essentially surjective. A fully faithful, essentially surjective functor is an equivalence.

concepts.c:complex-manifold: Holomorphic coordinates allow local integration, and $\mathcal O_X$ builds the inverse.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The bundle carries the connection and has local holomorphic frames.
concepts.c:flat-connection: Zero curvature makes the system for parallel sections integrable.
concepts.c:equivalence-of-categories: The theorem says that the functor is an equivalence of categories.
concepts.c:local-system: Horizontal sections of a flat bundle form a local system, and every local system arises.

source.note: The classical basic form of the correspondence, as in P. Deligne, Équations différentielles à points singuliers réguliers, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 163, Springer, 1970, chapter I; it needs the holomorphic Frobenius theorem.

statement: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be [consistent](c:consistency) [first-order theories](c:first-order-theory) in languages $L_1$ and $L_2$, and let $L = L_1 \cap L_2$. If a [complete theory](c:complete-theory) $T$ in $L$ follows from $T_1$ and from $T_2$, then $T_1 \cup T_2$ is consistent.

hypotheses.text: The theories $T_1$ and $T_2$ are [consistent](c:consistency) first-order theories in $L_1$ and $L_2$.
A [complete theory](c:complete-theory) $T$ in $L = L_1 \cap L_2$ follows from $T_1$ and from $T_2$.

conclusion: The union $T_1 \cup T_2$ has a model, so it is consistent in the language $L_1 \cup L_2$.

proofs.name: Via Craig interpolation
proofs.slogan: An inconsistency of the union gives two sentences that contradict each other, an interpolant in the common language splits them, and completeness of $T$ makes one theory inconsistent.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with sentences closed under conjunction. If the two sentences share no symbol, the interpolant uses equality only, and the proof is unchanged.

roles.why: [Consistency](c:consistency) of each $T_i$ is what the final contradiction violates.
[Completeness](c:complete-theory) of $T$ decides the interpolant, so one of $T_1$, $T_2$ proves its negation.

steps.slogan: Pick two sentences, one from each theory, that contradict each other.
steps.detail: Suppose $T_1 \cup T_2$ is inconsistent. By compactness a finite part is inconsistent, so taking conjunctions gives an $L_1$-sentence $\varphi_1$ implied by $T_1$ and an $L_2$-sentence $\varphi_2$ implied by $T_2$ with $\varphi_1 \models \neg\varphi_2$.

steps.slogan: Take an interpolant of the two sentences in the common language.
steps.detail: Craig interpolation applied to $\varphi_1 \models \neg\varphi_2$ gives an $L$-sentence $\theta$ with $\varphi_1 \models \theta$ and $\theta \models \neg\varphi_2$.

steps.slogan: Let the complete theory $T$ decide the interpolant.
steps.detail: Because $T$ is complete in $L$, either $\theta$ or $\neg\theta$ follows from $T$. Both $T_1$ and $T_2$ prove every sentence of $T$.

steps.slogan: Derive an inconsistency in $T_1$ or in $T_2$ from either case.
steps.detail:
If $T \models 	heta$, then $T_2 \models 	heta$, so $T_2 \models 
eg\varphi_2$, against $T_2 \models \varphi_2$ and consistency of $T_2$. If $T \models 
eg	heta$, then $T_1 \models 
eg	heta$ and $\varphi_1 \models 	heta$ give $T_1 \models 
eg\varphi_1$, against $T_1 \models \varphi_1$.

concepts.c:consistency: The proof assumes the union inconsistent and contradicts consistency of a $T_i$.
concepts.c:first-order-theory: The theories are sets of first-order sentences, to which compactness and Craig apply.
concepts.c:complete-theory: Completeness of $T$ forces $\theta$ or its negation into $T$.

source.note: The standard derivation of Robinson's joint consistency theorem from Craig interpolation; the two theorems are equivalent (see Chang and Keisler, Model Theory).

proofs.name: Elementary chains and amalgamation
proofs.slogan: Elementary equivalence of the common reducts lets two elementary chains alternate, and their unions are isomorphic over $L$, which gives one structure for both theories.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by a direct model construction that does not use interpolation. Every consistent theory has a model, by the completeness theorem.

roles.why: [Consistency](c:consistency) gives a model $A$ of $T_1$ and a model $B$ of $T_2$.
[Completeness](c:complete-theory) of $T$ makes the $L$-reducts of $A$ and $B$ [elementarily equivalent](c:elementary-equivalence).

steps.slogan: Take models of both theories and compare their common reducts.
steps.detail: Let $A \models T_1$ and $B \models T_2$. Both $L$-reducts satisfy the complete theory $T$, so $A|_L$ and $B|_L$ are elementarily equivalent.

steps.slogan: Extend one structure elementarily so that the other embeds $L$-elementarily.
steps.detail: If $A|_L \equiv B|_L$, the $L_2$-elementary diagram of $B$ together with the $L$-elementary diagram of $A$ is finitely satisfiable: a finite part about $A$ is an $L$-sentence true in $A|_L$, hence in $B|_L$. By compactness it has a model, an elementary extension $B' \succeq B$ with an $L$-[elementary embedding](c:elementary-embedding) $A|_L \to B'|_L$.

steps.slogan: Alternate the extension to build two elementary chains with $L$-elementary maps.
steps.detail: Start with $A_0 = A$ and $B_0 = B'$ from the previous step. Repeat it with the roles swapped and with constants for the previous structure, to get $A_n \preceq A_{n+1}$, $B_n \preceq B_{n+1}$ and $L$-elementary maps $f_n\colon A_n \to B_n$, $g_n\colon B_n \to A_{n+1}$ with $g_n f_n$ the inclusion of $A_n$ and $f_{n+1} g_n$ the inclusion of $B_n$.

steps.slogan: Take the unions of the chains and fit the maps into an $L$-isomorphism.
steps.detail: The unions $A^* = \bigcup A_n$ and $B^* = \bigcup B_n$ are elementary extensions of $A$ and $B$ by the elementary chain theorem, so $A^* \models T_1$ and $B^* \models T_2$. The maps $f_n$ and $g_n$ fit together to an isomorphism $f\colon A^*|_L \to B^*|_L$.

steps.slogan: Transport the $L_2$-structure of $B^*$ onto $A^*$ to get a model of both theories.
steps.detail: Pull the $L_2$-symbols back along $f$ to $A^*$. The resulting $(L_1 \cup L_2)$-structure has $L_1$-reduct $A^* \models T_1$ and $L_2$-reduct isomorphic to $B^* \models T_2$. So it is a model of $T_1 \cup T_2$.

concepts.c:consistency: Consistency of each theory gives the models that start the construction.
concepts.c:first-order-theory: The theories are the sets of sentences that the structures satisfy.
concepts.c:complete-theory: Completeness of $T$ makes the two common reducts agree on all $L$-sentences.
concepts.c:elementary-equivalence: Elementary equivalence of the reducts is the input of the extension step.
concepts.c:elementary-embedding: $L$-elementary maps between the chain members yield the isomorphism of the unions.

source.note: Robinson's elementary-chain proof, as in Chang and Keisler, Model Theory.

statement: Let $X \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and $Y \subseteq \mathbb R^m$ be open. Every continuous [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) $B$ on $C_c^\infty(X) \times C_c^\infty(Y)$ has the form $B(\varphi, \psi) = K(\varphi \otimes \psi)$ for a unique [distribution](c:distribution) $K$ on $X \times Y$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $X \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and $Y \subseteq \mathbb R^m$ are open.
The map $B$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) on the test functions that is continuous in each variable.

conclusion: There is exactly one [distribution](c:distribution) $K$ on $X \times Y$ with $B(\varphi, \psi) = K(\varphi \otimes \psi)$ for all test functions $\varphi, \psi$.

proofs.name: Bounds, localization and Fourier series
proofs.slogan: Continuity bounds the form by finitely many derivatives, a partition of unity reduces to cubes, and a Fourier series with polynomially bounded coefficients defines the kernel.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof (Hörmander, section 5.2); the analytic estimates rest on the cited text. Separate continuity of $B$ already gives joint continuity on Fréchet spaces.

roles.why: Open sets carry the test-function spaces and the [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) by cubes.
Continuity of the [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) gives the derivative bound that controls the coefficients.

steps.slogan: Turn continuity of the form into a bound by finitely many derivatives.
steps.detail: For compact $K_1 \subset X$ and $K_2 \subset Y$ the spaces $C^\infty_{K_1}$ and $C^\infty_{K_2}$ are Fréchet spaces. A separately continuous bilinear form on them is jointly continuous, so $|B(\varphi, \psi)| \le C \sum_{|\alpha|, |\beta| \le N} \sup|\partial^\alpha \varphi|\,\sup|\partial^\beta \psi|$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to test functions supported in cubes.
steps.detail: Cover $X$ and $Y$ by cubes and split test functions into finite sums of pieces supported in them, using a [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity). Kernels found on pairs of cubes glue to one kernel, by uniqueness, so one cube pair suffices.

steps.slogan: Expand cube-supported test functions in Fourier series.
steps.detail: A test function supported in a cube equals its Fourier series, whose coefficients decay faster than any power of the frequency. The bound of the first step shows that the values of $B$ on pairs of exponentials grow at most polynomially in the two frequencies.

steps.slogan: Define the kernel as a series of exponentials with polynomially bounded coefficients.
steps.detail: Set $K = \sum_{k,l} c_{kl}\, e_k \otimes e_l$, with $c_{kl}$ built from $B(e_k, e_l)$. Polynomial bounds make the series converge in the space of distributions, so $K$ is a [distribution](c:distribution) on the product.

steps.slogan: Check that $K$ represents $B$ and prove uniqueness by density.
steps.detail: Both $B(\varphi,\psi)$ and $K(\varphi \otimes \psi)$ are continuous in each variable and agree on the exponentials, so they agree on all test functions. Finite sums of tensors $\varphi \otimes \psi$ are dense in $C_c^\infty(X \times Y)$, so a distribution on the product is fixed by its values on tensors. This gives uniqueness.

concepts.c:bilinear-form: The kernel theorem represents this form by a single distribution.
concepts.c:distribution: The kernel is a distribution on the product, built as a convergent series.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: A partition of unity reduces the problem to cubes.

source.ref: L. Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I, Springer, 1983, section 5.2 (the kernel theorem); the theorem is due to L. Schwartz, Théorie des noyaux, Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians 1950, vol. 1 (1952), 220-230
source.note: Hörmander proves the theorem in section 5.2 from estimates on compact sets and an expansion in exponentials; a second route uses nuclearity of the test-function spaces.

statement: Let $X$ be a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) Hausdorff space, $Y$ a [Banach space](c:banach-space), and $F$ a [multivalued map](c:multivalued-map) from $X$ to the nonempty closed [convex](c:convex-set) subsets of $Y$ that is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuity). Then $F$ has a continuous selector: a continuous $f\colon X \to Y$ with $f(x) \in F(x)$ for every $x$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) Hausdorff space.
The space $Y$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space).
The map $F$ is [lower semicontinuous](c:lower-semicontinuity): for every open $W \subseteq Y$ the set $\{x : F(x) \cap W \ne \emptyset\}$ is open.
Every value $F(x)$ is nonempty, closed and [convex](c:convex-set).

conclusion: A continuous map $f\colon X \to Y$ exists with $f(x) \in F(x)$ for all $x \in X$.

proofs.name: Approximate selections and a uniform limit
proofs.slogan: Build continuous selectors that are $\varepsilon$-close to $F$ by a partition of unity, refine them with halving errors, and pass to the uniform limit.
proofs.scope: The record names the family of selection theorems; this proof treats its standard Banach-space instance, Michael's theorem. The values may be unbounded.

roles.why: [Paracompactness](c:paracompact-space) supplies a locally finite partition of unity subordinate to any open cover.
Completeness of the [Banach space](c:banach-space) makes the uniformly Cauchy sequence converge.
[Lower semicontinuity](c:lower-semicontinuity) makes the sets $\{x : y \in G(x)\}$ open and keeps the shrunken maps lower semicontinuous.
[Convexity](c:convex-set) lets averages of nearby points stay near $F(x)$, and closedness makes the limit lie in $F(x)$.

steps.slogan: Build a continuous $\varepsilon$-approximate selector for a lower semicontinuous convex-valued map.
steps.detail: Let $G(x) = \{y : d(y, F(x)) < \varepsilon\}$, which is nonempty and convex. The sets $U_y = \{x : y \in G(x)\}$ cover $X$ and are open, by lower semicontinuity applied to the ball $B(y, \varepsilon)$. A locally finite [partition of unity](c:partition-of-unity) $(\varphi_i)$ subordinate to $U_{y_i}$ gives $f = \sum \varphi_i y_i$, which is continuous and has $f(x) \in G(x)$ by convexity.

steps.slogan: Show that cutting $F$ by a moving ball keeps lower semicontinuity.
steps.detail: Let $f$ be continuous and $G(x) = F(x) \cap B(f(x), r)$. If $z \in G(x) \cap W$, put $\delta = r - |z - f(x)|$. The points $x'$ with $|f(x') - f(x)| < \delta/2$ and $F(x') \cap W \cap B(z, \delta/2) \ne \emptyset$ form a neighborhood of $x$, and for them $G(x')$ meets $W$.

steps.slogan: Refine the approximate selectors so that the errors halve at each stage.
steps.detail: Take $f_0$ from the first step with $\varepsilon = 1$. Given $f_n$ with $d(f_n(x), F(x)) < 2^{-n}$, apply the first step to $G_n(x) = F(x) \cap B(f_n(x), 2^{-n})$ with $\varepsilon = 2^{-n-1}$. This gives $f_{n+1}$ with $d(f_{n+1}(x), F(x)) < 2^{-n-1}$ and $\|f_{n+1}(x) - f_n(x)\| < 2^{1-n}$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the uniform limit and place its values in $F(x)$.
steps.detail: Since $\sum 2^{1-n} < \infty$, the sequence $(f_n)$ is uniformly Cauchy, and it converges uniformly to some $f$ because $Y$ is complete. The limit $f$ is continuous. As $d(f_n(x), F(x)) \to 0$, we get $d(f(x), F(x)) = 0$, so $f(x) \in F(x)$ because $F(x)$ is closed.

concepts.c:paracompact-space: Paracompactness provides the partition of unity that builds approximate selectors.
concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness gives the limit of the uniformly Cauchy selectors.
concepts.c:multivalued-map: The selector picks one value of the multivalued map $F$ at each point.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convex values allow averaging by a partition of unity.
concepts.c:lower-semicontinuity: It makes the preimage sets open, which the partition of unity needs.
concepts.c:partition-of-unity: Averaging over a partition of unity makes the approximate selector continuous.

source.note: Michael's proof, E. Michael, Continuous selections I, Annals of Mathematics 63 (1956), 361-382; the first step is also the approximate theorem proved in mathlib for open lower sections.

statement: The category of framed oriented [tangles](c:tangle) up to isotopy, with objects the finite sequences of signs, is a [ribbon category](c:ribbon-category). For every ribbon category $C$ and object $V$ of $C$ there is a unique ribbon functor from it to $C$ that sends the object $+$ to $V$.

hypotheses.text: The target $C$ is a [ribbon category](c:ribbon-category).
The object $V$ is an object of $C$.

conclusion: The category of framed oriented tangles is the free ribbon category on one object.

proofs.name: Generators, relations and the universal property
proofs.slogan: Framed tangles are generated by elementary tangles, isotopy follows from the ribbon axioms, so a ribbon functor is fixed by the image of one point.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published coherence theorem; the isotopy and Reidemeister analysis rests on the cited work.

roles.why: The [ribbon category](c:ribbon-category) structure of $C$ supplies the images of the cups, caps, crossings and twists, and its axioms give the isotopy moves.
The object $V$ is the image of the sign $+$, and all other values follow.

steps.slogan: Give the tangle category its ribbon structure.
steps.detail: Juxtaposition of tangles is the tensor product and the crossing is the braiding. Reversing orientation gives duals with the cup and cap as evaluation and coevaluation, and a full framing twist is the twist. Each ribbon axiom holds as an isotopy of framed tangles.

steps.slogan: Present every framed oriented tangle as a composite of elementary tangles.
steps.detail: A generic projection and a slicing by height show that every [tangle](c:tangle) is isotopic to a composite of tensor products of identities, cups, caps, crossings and twists. So these elementary tangles generate all morphisms.

steps.slogan: Show that isotopic composites of elementary tangles differ only by ribbon axioms.
steps.detail: Two such composites are isotopic exactly when they are related by planar isotopy and framed Reidemeister-type moves. The cited work shows that each move holds in every [ribbon category](c:ribbon-category) as a consequence of its axioms.

steps.slogan: Define the functor into $C$ on elementary tangles and extend it.
steps.detail: Send $+$ to $V$, the sign $-$ to the dual of $V$, and the elementary tangles to the matching structure maps of $C$. The previous step shows that the assignment respects isotopy, so it is well defined, and it preserves tensor, braiding, duals and twist.

steps.slogan: Show that a ribbon functor is determined by the image of $+$.
steps.detail: A ribbon functor preserves tensor, braiding, duals and twist, so its values on the elementary tangles are forced by its value on $+$. These tangles generate every morphism, so two ribbon functors that agree on $+$ are equal. Hence the functor above is the unique one.

concepts.c:tangle: Tangles are the morphisms that the elementary tangles generate.
concepts.c:ribbon-category: The ribbon axioms are the relations between elementary tangles.

source.ref: M. C. Shum, Tortile tensor categories, Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra 93 (1994), 57-110
source.note: Shum proves that the free tortile (ribbon) category on one object is the category of framed oriented tangles.

statement: Let $I$ be a [small category](c:small-category) and $F\colon I \to \mathrm{sSet}$ a [diagram](c:diagram) of [simplicial sets](c:simplicial-set). Let $BF$ be its bar construction, the diagram $j \mapsto \big|[n] \mapsto \coprod_{i_0 \to \cdots \to i_n \to j} F(i_0)\big|$. Then $BF \to F$ is an objectwise [weak equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence), $BF$ is [cofibrant](c:cofibrant-object), and $\operatorname{colim} BF$ is the [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) of $F$.

hypotheses.text: The indexing category $I$ is a [small category](c:small-category).
The functor $F\colon I \to \mathrm{sSet}$ is a [diagram](c:diagram) of [simplicial sets](c:simplicial-set).

conclusion: The bar construction is a cofibrant replacement of $F$ in the projective structure, and its colimit is the [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) of $F$.

proofs.name: Extra degeneracy and free diagrams
proofs.slogan: The simplices over each object form a nerve with a terminal object, which contracts the bar construction to the diagram, and each level is a free diagram.
proofs.scope: Diagrams of simplicial sets with the projective model structure; the same proof works in any simplicial model category. The realization is the diagonal of the bisimplicial set.

roles.why: A small indexing category makes the coproducts over chains of arrows and the free diagrams well defined.
The diagram $F$ supplies the simplicial sets $F(i_0)$ and the augmentation to $F(j)$.

steps.slogan: Form the simplicial replacement of $F$ over each object and its augmentation.
steps.detail: Put $N_nF(j) = \coprod_{i_0 \to \cdots \to i_n \to j} F(i_0)$, with faces that compose arrows or apply $F$ and degeneracies that insert identities. Maps in $j$ make it a diagram, and $F(i_0) \to F(j)$ along the last arrow gives an augmentation $\varepsilon_j$. The bar construction $BF$ is the diagonal.

steps.slogan: Build an extra degeneracy from the terminal object of the slice category.
steps.detail: The simplices over $j$ are the chains of the slice category $I{\downarrow}j$, which has the terminal object $(j, \mathrm{id}_j)$. Appending $\mathrm{id}_j$ at the end of a string defines $s\colon N_nF(j) \to N_{n+1}F(j)$ with $d_{n+1}s = \mathrm{id}$ and $d_k s = s\,d_k$ for $k \le n$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the augmentation is a weak equivalence for every object $j$.
steps.detail: In each simplicial degree $k$ the augmented simplicial set $N_\bullet F(j)_k \to F(j)_k$ has an extra degeneracy, so it is a homotopy equivalence on realizations. A map of bisimplicial sets that is a weak equivalence in one direction in each degree is one on diagonals, so $\varepsilon_j\colon BF(j) \to F(j)$ is a [weak equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).

steps.slogan: Show that $BF$ is a projectively cofibrant diagram.
steps.detail: Level $n$ of $N_\bullet F$ is the coproduct over chains of $F(i_0) \times I(i_n, -)$, a free diagram on a simplicial set, hence projectively [cofibrant](c:cofibrant-object). Degeneracies are inclusions of summands, so $N_\bullet F$ is Reedy cofibrant and its diagonal $BF$ is cofibrant.

steps.slogan: Identify the colimit of $BF$ with the Bousfield-Kan homotopy colimit of $F$.
steps.detail: Colimits commute with coproducts and diagonals, and $\operatorname{colim}_j I(i_n, j) = *$. So $\operatorname{colim} BF$ is the diagonal of $[n] \mapsto \coprod_{i_0 \to \cdots \to i_n} F(i_0)$, the Bousfield-Kan [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit). Since $BF \to F$ is a cofibrant replacement, this is the derived [colimit](c:colimit) of $F$.

concepts.c:small-category: Smallness lets coproducts over chains of arrows exist and the free diagrams be defined.
concepts.c:diagram: The construction replaces a diagram by a cofibrant one.
concepts.c:simplicial-set: The values $F(i)$ and all the levels of the construction are simplicial sets.
concepts.c:weak-homotopy-equivalence: The comparison $BF \to F$ must be a weak equivalence, so that $BF$ replaces $F$.
concepts.c:cofibrant-object: Cofibrancy makes the colimit of $BF$ the derived colimit.
concepts.c:homotopy-colimit: The colimit of the cofibrant replacement is the homotopy colimit.
concepts.c:colimit: The colimit of a free diagram is computed levelwise.

source.note: The standard argument, as in A. K. Bousfield and D. M. Kan, Homotopy limits, completions and localizations, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 304, Springer, 1972, chapter XII, and P. S. Hirschhorn, Model categories and their localizations, AMS, 2003, chapter 18.

statement: For every [complex number](c:complex-number) $z$, the [power series](c:power-series) $\sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n z^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!$ converges absolutely, and its sum is $\sin z$.

hypotheses.text: The input $z$ is a [complex number](c:complex-number).

proofs.name: Odd part of the exponential series
proofs.slogan: Write the sine through two exponentials, expand both by the exponential series, and keep the odd terms, since the even terms cancel.
proofs.scope: Every complex $z$, including $z = 0$. The even-index terms cancel exactly, so the regrouping by parity is justified by absolute convergence.

roles.why: The [exponential series](c:exponential-function) converges absolutely for every complex argument, so the regrouping is allowed.

steps.slogan: Write the sine as a difference of two complex exponentials.
steps.detail: By definition, $\sin z = i\,(e^{-iz} - e^{iz})/2$, where $e^w$ is the complex exponential function. The next step expands both exponentials.

steps.slogan: Expand both exponentials by the exponential series and subtract.
steps.detail: For every complex $w$, $e^w = \sum_k w^k/k!$ with absolute convergence. Subtracting the series for $w = iz$ and $w = -iz$ gives $\sin z = \sum_k i\big((-iz)^k - (iz)^k\big)/(2\,k!)$.

steps.slogan: Split the indices by parity and drop the even terms.
steps.detail: Write $k = 2n + r$ with $r \in \{0, 1\}$, a bijection of $\mathbb N$ with $\mathbb N \times \{0,1\}$. For $r = 0$ the two powers $(\mp iz)^{2n}$ are equal, so the term vanishes. A convergent series can be summed in fibres over $n$, so $\sin z = \sum_n -i\,(iz)^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!$.

steps.slogan: Simplify the odd terms to $(-1)^n z^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!$.
steps.detail: Since $(iz)^{2n+1} = i\,(-1)^n z^{2n+1}$, the factor in front becomes $-i \cdot i\,(-1)^n = (-1)^n$. Hence $\sin z = \sum_n (-1)^n z^{2n+1}/(2n+1)!$, and the series converges absolutely because the exponential series does.

concepts.c:complex-number: The identity holds for every complex argument, since the exponential series always converges.
concepts.c:power-series: The sine is expanded as a power series in $z$ with infinite radius.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The sine is built from two exponentials, and its series is their odd part.

source.note: mathlib subtracts two copies of the exponential series (expSeries_div_hasSum_exp), regroups by parity with Nat.divModEquiv in Complex.hasSum_sin', and simplifies powers of $i$.

statement: Let $X$ be a finite [CW-spectrum](c:cw-spectrum) in the stable homotopy category. Then $X$ is [dualizable](c:dualizable-object) for the [smash product](c:smash-product): with $DX = F(X, S)$ the function spectrum into the sphere spectrum, the natural map $DX \wedge Y \to F(X, Y)$ is an equivalence for every spectrum $Y$.

hypotheses.text: The [CW-spectrum](c:cw-spectrum) $X$ has finitely many cells.

conclusion: The spectrum $X$ has a dual $DX$, with evaluation $DX \wedge X \to S$ and coevaluation $S \to X \wedge DX$ that satisfy the triangle identities.

proofs.name: Induction on cells
proofs.slogan: Compare $DX \wedge Y$ with $F(X, Y)$ by a natural map, check it on spheres, and extend over cofiber sequences by the five lemma, cell by cell.
proofs.scope: Finite spectra in the stable homotopy category, a closed symmetric monoidal triangulated category. The zero spectrum has no cells and is trivially dualizable.

roles.why: Finitely many cells make an induction on the number of cells reach the whole spectrum $X$.

steps.slogan: Define the natural comparison map from $DX \wedge Y$ to $F(X, Y)$.
steps.detail: The evaluation $F(X, S) \wedge X \to S$ and the closed monoidal structure give a natural map $\nu\colon F(X,S) \wedge Y \to F(X,Y)$. Both sides are exact contravariant functors of $X$, and $\nu$ is a natural transformation between them.

steps.slogan: Check that the comparison map is an equivalence for each sphere $S^n$.
steps.detail: For $X = S^n$ we have $F(S^n, S) = S^{-n}$. Both $S^{-n} \wedge Y$ and $F(S^n, Y)$ are the desuspension $\Sigma^{-n}Y$, and $\nu$ is the identity between them.

steps.slogan: Show that equivalences of the comparison map pass along cofiber sequences.
steps.detail: A cofiber sequence $X' \to X \to X''$ gives long exact sequences of homotopy groups for both sides, natural in the sequence. If $\nu$ is an equivalence for two of the three spectra, the five lemma gives it for the third.

steps.slogan: Induct on the number of cells of $X$ to cover every finite spectrum.
steps.detail: A finite [CW-spectrum](c:cw-spectrum) is built from spheres by finitely many cell attachments, each a cofiber of a map out of a sphere. The sphere step and the cofiber step prove by induction that $\nu$ is an equivalence for all $Y$.

steps.slogan: Read off the evaluation, the coevaluation and the triangle identities.
steps.detail: Taking $Y = X$ gives $DX \wedge X \simeq F(X, X)$, so the identity of $X$ corresponds to a coevaluation $S \to X \wedge DX$. The triangle identities follow from naturality of $\nu$ in $Y$ and the Yoneda lemma. So $X$ is [dualizable](c:dualizable-object) with dual $DX$.

concepts.c:cw-spectrum: A finite cell structure allows induction on the number of cells.
concepts.c:smash-product: Duality is taken with respect to the smash product of spectra.
concepts.c:dualizable-object: Dualizable means that the comparison map is an equivalence, which gives evaluation and coevaluation.

source.note: The standard induction on cells for Spanier-Whitehead duality (Spanier and Whitehead, 1955); see Adams, Stable Homotopy and Generalised Homology, part III.

statement: Let $G$ be a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group) with an inner regular [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) $\mu$, and let $E \subseteq G$ be a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) with $\mu(E) > 0$. Then the [difference set](c:difference-set) $EE^{-1}$ is a neighborhood of the identity. For $G = \mathbb R$ this says that $E - E$ contains an interval around $0$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group).
The measure $\mu$ is a left [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) on $G$ that is inner regular.
The set $E$ is a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) of $G$.
The measure of $E$ is positive: $\mu(E) > 0$.

conclusion: The set $EE^{-1} = \{xy^{-1} : x, y \in E\}$ contains an open neighborhood of the identity of $G$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the result multiplicatively, for $E/E$, and does not assume that $G$ is Hausdorff. Its additive twin gives $E - E$ as a neighborhood of $0$.

proofs.name: Compact subset and overlapping translates
proofs.slogan: Take a compact subset of positive measure, move it slightly so that it still nearly fills the same open set, and conclude that the translate overlaps it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any group element $g$ in a small neighborhood of the identity. Infinite measure of $E$ is allowed, because only a compact subset is used.

roles.why: Local compactness and the group topology give a neighborhood $V$ of the identity with $VK \subseteq U$.
Inner regularity gives the compact set, regularity of $\mu$ gives the open set, and left invariance gives $\mu(gK) = \mu(K)$.
Measurability of $E$ lets inner regularity find a compact subset of $E$.
Positive measure of $E$ yields a compact subset of positive measure.

steps.slogan: Choose a compact subset $K \subseteq E$ of positive measure.
steps.detail: Inner regularity of $\mu$ and $\mu(E) > 0$ give a compact $K \subseteq E$ with $\mu(K) > 0$. Replace $K$ by its closure, which is compact, lies in $E$ and has the same measure.

steps.slogan: Enclose $K$ in an open set of almost the same measure.
steps.detail: Since $K$ is compact, $\mu(K) < \infty$. Regularity of $\mu$ gives an open set $U \supseteq K$ with $\mu(U \setminus K) < \mu(K)$.

steps.slogan: Find a neighborhood $V$ of the identity with $gK \subseteq U$ for all $g \in V$.
steps.detail: The compact set $K$ lies in the open set $U$. By continuity of multiplication there is a neighborhood $V$ of $1$ with $VK \subseteq U$. For $g \in V$ this gives $\mu(gK \setminus K) \le \mu(U \setminus K) < \mu(K)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $gK$ meets $K$ for every $g \in V$.
steps.detail: If $gK \cap K = \emptyset$, then left invariance gives $\mu(gK \setminus K) = \mu(gK) = \mu(K)$, against the bound of the previous step. So some $x \in K$ has $gx \in K$.

steps.slogan: Write $g = (gx)x^{-1}$ to place $V$ inside $EE^{-1}$.
steps.detail: Both $gx$ and $x$ lie in $K \subseteq E$, so $g = (gx)x^{-1} \in EE^{-1}$ for every $g \in V$. Hence $V \subseteq EE^{-1}$, and $EE^{-1}$ is a neighborhood of $1$.

concepts.c:locally-compact-group: The group topology lets small translates of $K$ stay inside $U$.
concepts.c:haar-measure: Left invariance of the measure makes translates of $K$ have the same measure.
concepts.c:measurable-set: Measurable sets are the ones that inner regularity approximates from inside.
concepts.c:difference-set: The set $EE^{-1}$ is the set that must contain a neighborhood of the identity.

source.note: mathlib takes a compact subset of positive measure (MeasurableSet.exists_lt_isCompact), makes translates nearly equal to it in measure (eventually_nhds_one_measure_smul_sdiff_lt), and reads off the quotient from an overlap (steinhaus_mul_aux).

statement: Let $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ be real sequences with $(b_n)$ strictly increasing and $b_n \to +\infty$. If the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $L = \lim_{n} \dfrac{a_{n+1} - a_n}{b_{n+1} - b_n}$ exists as a real number, then $\dfrac{a_n}{b_n} \to L$.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $(b_n)$ is a strictly increasing [monotone sequence](c:monotone-sequence) with $b_n \to +\infty$.
The quotients $(a_{n+1} - a_n)/(b_{n+1} - b_n)$ have a real [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $L$.

conclusion: The quotients $a_n / b_n$ converge, and their limit is $L$.

proofs.name: Telescoped bounds
proofs.slogan: Bound each difference quotient near $L$, add the bounds from a fixed index, divide by $b_n$, and let $n$ and then the tolerance tend to their limits.
proofs.scope: The case of a finite limit $L$. For $L = +\infty$ the same sum gives only the lower bound, with a large $M$ in place of $L - \varepsilon$, and this already forces $a_n/b_n \to +\infty$; the case $L = -\infty$ is symmetric.

roles.why: Strict growth makes every $b_{k+1} - b_k$ positive, so the inequalities keep their direction, and $b_n \to \infty$ makes the boundary terms vanish.
The [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $L$ puts every difference quotient beyond $N$ inside $(L - \varepsilon, L + \varepsilon)$.

steps.slogan: Bound every difference quotient beyond an index $N$ within $\varepsilon$ of $L$.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $N$ with $L - \varepsilon < (a_{k+1} - a_k)/(b_{k+1} - b_k) < L + \varepsilon$ for $k \ge N$. Since $b_{k+1} - b_k > 0$, this means $(L - \varepsilon)(b_{k+1} - b_k) < a_{k+1} - a_k < (L + \varepsilon)(b_{k+1} - b_k)$.

steps.slogan: Add the bounds for $k = N, \dots, n-1$ and telescope both sides.
steps.detail: The sums of $a_{k+1} - a_k$ and of $b_{k+1} - b_k$ telescope, so $(L - \varepsilon)(b_n - b_N) < a_n - a_N < (L + \varepsilon)(b_n - b_N)$ for every $n > N$.

steps.slogan: Divide by $b_n$ to compare $a_n/b_n$ with $L \pm \varepsilon$.
steps.detail: For $n$ large we have $b_n > 0$, and the previous inequality gives $(L - \varepsilon)\big(1 - b_N/b_n\big) + a_N/b_n < a_n/b_n < (L + \varepsilon)\big(1 - b_N/b_n\big) + a_N/b_n$.

steps.slogan: Let $n \to \infty$ to trap the limits of $a_n/b_n$ near $L$.
steps.detail: Since $b_n \to \infty$, both $b_N/b_n$ and $a_N/b_n$ tend to $0$, so the two bounds tend to $L - \varepsilon$ and $L + \varepsilon$. Hence $L - \varepsilon \le \liminf a_n/b_n \le \limsup a_n/b_n \le L + \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon \to 0$ to conclude that $a_n/b_n$ tends to $L$.
steps.detail: The last inequalities hold for every $\varepsilon > 0$, so $\liminf a_n/b_n$ and $\limsup a_n/b_n$ both equal $L$. Hence the sequence converges to $L$.

concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The hypothesis and the conclusion are limits, handled by $\varepsilon$ bounds.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotone growth of $b_n$ fixes the sign of every denominator.

source.note: The standard proof of the Stolz-Cesàro theorem by summing the difference quotient bounds, as in textbooks of real analysis.

statement: A finite simple [graph](c:graph) $G$ is [perfect](c:perfect-graph), that is $\chi(H) = \omega(H)$ for every [induced subgraph](c:induced-subgraph) $H$, if and only if neither $G$ nor its complement has an induced odd cycle of length at least $5$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is a finite simple [graph](c:graph).

conclusion: The graph $G$ is perfect exactly when it has no odd hole and no odd antihole.

proofs.name: Decomposition of Berge graphs
proofs.slogan: Odd holes and antiholes are imperfect, and a minimal imperfect Berge graph would be basic or decomposable, which the structure theorem and the analysis of decompositions rule out.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the decomposition theorem for Berge graphs is the long part and rests on the cited paper. A Berge graph is a graph with no odd hole and no odd antihole.

roles.why: A finite [graph](c:graph) has a minimal imperfect induced subgraph if it is imperfect, which starts the minimal counterexample argument.

steps.slogan: Show that a perfect graph has no odd hole and no odd antihole.
steps.detail: An odd hole $C_{2k+1}$ with $k \ge 2$ has [clique](c:clique) number $2$ and [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) $3$. An odd antihole on $2k+1$ vertices has clique number $k$ and chromatic number $k+1$. Perfection passes to [induced subgraphs](c:induced-subgraph), so a perfect graph contains neither.

steps.slogan: Prove that the basic classes of Berge graphs are perfect.
steps.detail: Bipartite graphs, line graphs of bipartite graphs and the complements of both are perfect. König's theorems give the colouring equalities, and the perfect graph theorem passes perfection to complements. The cited work checks the remaining basic class, the double split graphs.

steps.slogan: State the decomposition theorem for Berge graphs.
steps.detail: The cited paper proves that every Berge graph is basic, or has a 2-join, or its complement has a 2-join, or it has a balanced skew partition. This is the long and difficult part of the proof.

steps.slogan: Show that a minimal imperfect Berge graph has none of these decompositions.
steps.detail: The cited work, with earlier results on 2-joins and skew partitions, shows that a minimal imperfect Berge graph admits no 2-join, no 2-join in its complement and no balanced skew partition. The perfect graph theorem makes the complement of a minimal imperfect graph minimal imperfect too.

steps.slogan: Combine the steps in a minimal counterexample argument.
steps.detail: Suppose a Berge graph is imperfect and take one with fewest vertices, so it is minimal imperfect. By the decomposition theorem it is basic, hence perfect, or it has a decomposition that the previous step excludes. This contradiction, with the first step, proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem is about finite simple graphs and their complements.
concepts.c:perfect-graph: Perfection is the property that the odd holes and antiholes obstruct.
concepts.c:induced-subgraph: Perfection is defined on all induced subgraphs, and holes are induced subgraphs.
concepts.c:clique: The clique number is the lower bound for the chromatic number.
concepts.c:chromatic-number: The chromatic number exceeds the clique number on odd holes and antiholes.

source.ref: M. Chudnovsky, N. Robertson, P. Seymour and R. Thomas, The strong perfect graph theorem, Annals of Mathematics 164 (2006), 51-229
source.note: The paper proves the structure theorem for Berge graphs and combines it with earlier results on decompositions.

statement: For every flowchart program $P$ with finitely many assignment and test boxes there is a program $P'$ built only from sequence, selection (if-then-else) and iteration (while), with one extra integer variable, that computes the same function as $P$.

hypotheses.text: The program $P$ is a flowchart, a [control-flow graph](c:control-flow-graph) with finitely many assignment and test boxes.

conclusion: The program $P'$ halts on the same inputs as $P$ and leaves the same values in the variables of $P$, so structured programs compute every [computable function](c:computable-function) that flowcharts compute.

proofs.name: Program counter and one loop
proofs.slogan: Number the boxes of the flowchart, store the next box in a counter variable, and run a single while loop whose body is a chain of selections on the counter.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for terminating and non-terminating runs alike. The extra counter variable is part of the statement.

roles.why: Finitely many boxes of the [control-flow graph](c:control-flow-graph) give a finite chain of selections in the loop body.

steps.slogan: Number the boxes of the flowchart and list the successors of each box.
steps.detail: Number the boxes $1, \dots, n$, with box $1$ the entry and the label $0$ the exit. An assignment box $k$ has one successor $s(k)$. A test box $k$ has a condition $c_k$ and two successors $t(k)$ and $e(k)$.

steps.slogan: Add a program counter variable that records the next box to run.
steps.detail: Add a fresh integer variable $pc$. The state of $P'$ is the pair of the old variables and $pc$, and $pc = 0$ means halt. The aim is to keep this pair equal to the state of $P$ at the entry of its current box.

steps.slogan: Write a loop body that runs the box chosen by the counter.
steps.detail: The body is a chain of selections: if $pc = 1$ then run box $1$ and update $pc$, else if $pc = 2$ then run box $2$ and update $pc$, and so on up to $n$. An assignment box sets $pc := s(k)$, and a test box does a selection: if $c_k$ then $pc := t(k)$ else $pc := e(k)$.

steps.slogan: Wrap the body in one while loop that stops when the counter is zero.
steps.detail: Let $P'$ be the program $pc := 1$; while $pc \ne 0$ do body. It uses sequence, selection and one iteration, and no other control structure.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction that each pass of the loop simulates one box of $P$.
steps.detail: Before the $t$th pass, the pair of variables and $pc$ equals the state of $P$ about to run its $t$th box, with $pc = 0$ exactly when $P$ has halted. One pass runs that box and sets $pc$ to the next box, so the claim holds for $t + 1$. Hence $P'$ halts exactly when $P$ halts, with equal values.

concepts.c:control-flow-graph: The flowchart is the control-flow graph that the construction rewrites.
concepts.c:computable-function: Flowcharts compute all computable functions, so the structured form does too.

source.note: The folklore program-counter construction, discussed in D. Harel, On folk theorems, Communications of the ACM 23 (1980); the original theorem is C. Böhm and G. Jacopini, Communications of the ACM 9 (1966).

statement: For real numbers $a$ and $d$ and a natural number $n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms of the [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression) $a, a + d, a + 2d, \dots$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (a + kd) = \dfrac{n\,(2a + (n-1)d)}{2}$. In particular $0 + 1 + \cdots + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2$.

hypotheses.text: The terms are $a + kd$ for $k = 0, \dots, n-1$, with real numbers $a$ and $d$.
The number of terms $n$ is a [natural number](c:natural-number); for $n = 0$ the sum is empty and equals $0$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the case $a = 0$, $d = 1$, in the natural numbers with truncated division. The general formula follows by linearity of the finite sum.

proofs.name: Gauss pairing by reversal
proofs.slogan: Write the sum forwards and backwards, add the two copies termwise to get a constant, and divide the total by two.
proofs.scope: The whole formula, including $n = 0$ where both sides are $0$. Division by $2$ is allowed over the real numbers.

roles.why: The terms $a + kd$ pair up as $(a + kd) + (a + (n-1-k)d) = 2a + (n-1)d$.
A natural number $n$ of terms makes the reversal $k \mapsto n-1-k$ a bijection of the index set, and the constant sums to $n$ times itself.

steps.slogan: Write the sum a second time with the index order reversed.
steps.detail: Let $S = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (a + kd)$. The map $k \mapsto n-1-k$ is a bijection of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, so $S = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (a + (n-1-k)d)$ and $2S$ is the sum of the two copies.

steps.slogan: Add the two copies termwise to get the same constant in every position.
steps.detail: For each $k$, $(a + kd) + (a + (n-1-k)d) = 2a + (n-1)d$, which does not depend on $k$.

steps.slogan: Sum the constant over the $n$ positions.
steps.detail: A constant summed over $n$ positions is $n$ times that constant, so $2S = n\,(2a + (n-1)d)$.

steps.slogan: Divide by two and specialize to $a = 0$ and $d = 1$.
steps.detail: Dividing by $2$ gives $S = n(2a + (n-1)d)/2$. For $a = 0$ and $d = 1$ this is $\sum_{i<n} i = n(n-1)/2$; in the natural numbers the product $n(n-1)$ is even, so the division is exact.

concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: The terms of the sum form an arithmetic progression with constant difference.
concepts.c:natural-number: The number of terms is a natural number, so the sum is finite.

source.note: mathlib proves the doubled sum in sum_range_id_mul_two with Finset.sum_range_reflect, sum_add_distrib and sum_const, then cancels the factor 2.

statement: Let $f_n(k)$ and $g(k)$ be complex numbers for $n \in \mathbb N$ and $k \in \mathbb N$. Suppose $f_n(k) \to g(k)$ as $n \to \infty$ for every $k$, and $|f_n(k)| \le b_k$ for all $n$ and $k$, where $\sum_k b_k$ converges. Then $\sum_k f_n(k) \to \sum_k g(k)$ as $n \to \infty$.

hypotheses.text: For every $k$ the [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $f_n(k) \to g(k)$ holds as $n \to \infty$.
The bound $|f_n(k)| \le b_k$ holds for all $n$ and $k$ (eventually in $n$ suffices).
The series $\sum_k b_k$ converges, so $b$ is a [summable bound](c:summable-bound).

conclusion: The sums $\sum_k f_n(k)$ converge to $\sum_k g(k)$ as $n \to \infty$, and both series converge absolutely.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any index set, any complete normed group and any filter in place of $n \to \infty$. It needs the bound only eventually in $n$.

proofs.name: Three-epsilon split
proofs.slogan: Dominate the tails by the tail of the summable bound, pass to the limit in a finite part, and add three errors of size one third.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for the index set $\mathbb N$ and the limit $n \to \infty$. The pointwise limit $g$ also satisfies the bound, which gives absolute convergence of $\sum g$.

roles.why: The pointwise [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) makes the finite part converge and passes the bound to $g$.
The domination by $b_k$ controls every tail of $f_n$ uniformly in $n$.
A [summable bound](c:summable-bound) has small tails, so a finite set $T$ captures almost all of the sum.

steps.slogan: Pass the bound to the limit function and get absolute convergence.
steps.detail: For fixed $k$, the inequality $|f_n(k)| \le b_k$ passes to the limit and gives $|g(k)| \le b_k$. By the comparison test, $\sum_k g(k)$ and every $\sum_k f_n(k)$ converge absolutely.

steps.slogan: Choose a finite index set whose omitted tail of $b$ is small.
steps.detail: Fix $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\sum_k b_k$ converges, some finite set $T \subseteq \mathbb N$ has $\sum_{k \notin T} b_k < \varepsilon/3$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit in the finite sum over $T$.
steps.detail: A finite sum of convergent sequences converges to the sum of the limits. So for $n$ large, $\big|\sum_{k \in T} f_n(k) - \sum_{k \in T} g(k)\big| < \varepsilon/3$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tails of $f_n$ and of $g$ by the tail of $b$.
steps.detail: For every $n$, $\big|\sum_{k \notin T} f_n(k)\big| \le \sum_{k \notin T} b_k < \varepsilon/3$. The same bound holds for $g$, by the first step.

steps.slogan: Split the difference into three parts and add their bounds.
steps.detail: Write $\sum_k f_n(k) - \sum_k g(k) = \sum_{T} (f_n - g) + \sum_{T^c} f_n - \sum_{T^c} g$. The triangle inequality bounds its size by $\varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon$ for $n$ large.

concepts.c:limit-of-a-sequence: The hypothesis and the conclusion are limits of sequences in $n$.
concepts.c:summable-bound: A summable dominating sequence gives small tails uniform in $n$.

source.note: mathlib passes the bound to the limit (h_g_le), picks a finite set with small tail of the bound, and closes with the same three-epsilon estimate (Metric.tendsto_nhds, tendsto_finsetSum, norm_tsum_le_tsum_norm).
